question: Does the month of Rajab have special virtues, fasts or prayers?
asked: A sister is having a debate with some of her family members regarding the month of Rajab. They are quoting a lot of hadith about the blessings of Rajab, and she heard from somebody online that all of these hadith are not authentic. She said this to her relative, and it resulted in a huge argument with other members of her family. What should be done?
answer:
The answer consists of two parts. Firstly, the question of Rajab: are there any blessings of Rajab? For these types of questions we should always look to our famous icons of Islam, the people who are universally respected, the giants of our tradition, people like Ibn Hajar, al-Nawawi, al-Ghazali, Ibn Taymiyyah, and see what they have said about this issue.

With regards to the month of Rajab: without a doubt, Rajab is one of the four sacred months, al-ashhur al-hurum. And this means that it is the only month that is standalone. The other three months are... who knows? There are four hurum months... Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah and Muharram. By the way, everybody should know this; this is a part of our basic Shari'ah knowledge.

"Inna 'iddat al-shuhur 'ind Allah ithna 'ashara shahran": the number of months (this is in the Qur'an), the number of months that Allah has decreed, is twelve. "Fi kitabillah": this is in the Book of Allah, meaning in al-Lawh al-Mahfuz. The day He created the heavens and the earth, Allah declared there should be twelve months. "Minha arba'atun hurum": four of them are hurum months. Three of those four are connected, Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah and Muharram, and one is standalone. This is the month we are in. So this month does have that blessing, without a doubt.

Now, does it have any other blessing? The six books of hadith, the famous books, do not mention any hadith about the blessings of Rajab. And that's why pretty much the vast majority of our scholars have said that the month of Rajab does not have any other blessing than being a holy month. It is a blessed month, and in the blessed month you don't engage in warfare. In the days where war was going on, you do not engage in war that you initiate. Obviously you defend, but offensive, no. And overall, you can do any good deeds in these four months; it is a more respected month. But specifically, any good deed mentioned? Many scholars say no.

Ibn Hajar says: "Nothing authentic has been narrated regarding the blessings of Rajab, or the fasting of Rajab, or any type of qiyam al-layl in Rajab. And I'm not the only one to say so; Abu Isma'il al-Harawi, the great hafidh, also says the same thing." So Ibn Hajar is saying this. Ibn Taymiyyah says that as for fasting in the month of Rajab, all of the traditions that are quoted are very weak; in fact they are fabricated, and none of the people of knowledge have ever considered them to be worthy. So there are some hadith; as Ibn Taymiyyah says, all of them are fabricated or very weak. So there are some of them, but generally speaking, our mainstream 'ulama have considered these to be extremely weak.

I'll mention some of the narrations. And remember, I told you all of you should know (and one of the goals of this Q&A is to educate all of us): this is our knowledge, our religion, our Shari'ah, our books of hadith. So by attending these lectures, I want to increase the general awareness of our religion.

I mentioned many times that the books of hadith are a confusing thing for the non-specialist, because there are so many of them. And I said that you should be aware that, simplistically, there are three tiers of hadith books. You have the elite, the crème de la crème: these are called the six books, al-Kutub al-Sittah, and you can add to them Musnad Imam Ahmad and Muwatta' Imam Malik. These are the famous books. You have a secondary level, and these are like the Mustadrak of al-Hakim, Bayhaqi, al-Darimi, al-Daraqutni. These are names that are very familiar to all students of knowledge, and especially 'ulama; they accessed them. Then you have the tertiary books. These are, without exaggeration, hundreds. Hundreds, not dozens, no exaggeration: little treatises, pamphlets, major volumes. And this is where you get every bizarre and weird type of thing.

Not that you don't find them in the secondary, but generally speaking, in the primary you don't find anything really bizarre; that's why they've been accepted by the ummah. The secondary, maybe once in a while you find something, but generally they're very good resources. The tertiary level: even advanced 'ulama generally don't have all of the books, and they haven't even heard of all of them, and they know they haven't heard of all of them. That's fine; that's the way it goes. Only those that are really, really specialists in hadith would be familiar with most of them. All of them is really impossible to be fully familiar with.

So in these books we have, for example, al-Tabarani in his al-Awsat (and al-Awsat is one of the more tertiary books, because Tabarani has multiple books; al-Tabarani in his Kabir might be secondary, but al-Awsat is definitely tertiary), and you have Abu Nu'aym in his Hilyah, which is again one of the tertiary books. He has a hadith of Anas ibn Malik that allegedly the Prophet ﷺ would say, when Rajab comes in: "Allahumma barik lana fi Rajab wa Sha'ban wa ballighna Ramadan."

In this there are two people in the chain. One of them, his name is Za'idah ibn Abi al-Ruqad. Bukhari says Za'idah is munkar al-hadith. If Bukhari says munkar, you literally just take this and leave it aside. When Bukhari says munkar, end of story; it's basically fabricated. So Imam al-Bukhari said the main guy narrating this hadith is rejected. Munkar means he's totally rejected. And if you know anything about Bukhari, that's it, end of case. So the famous narration "Allahumma barik lana fi Rajab wa Sha'ban wa ballighna Ramadan" is not a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ.

The translation is: "O Allah, bless us in Rajab, and bless us in Sha'ban, and allow us to reach Ramadan." This is not a hadith. Question to you: is there anything wrong with this hadith, meaning-wise? No. So can we say it? Why can we not say it, when there's nothing wrong with the meaning, as long as we don't attribute it to the Prophet ﷺ? It's not a hadith, but the meaning is beautiful: O Allah, bless us in Rajab; in the month of Rajab, bless us. O Allah, bless us in the month of Sha'ban. O Allah, allow us to live to see Ramadan. No problem to say it, but don't consider it to be a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ.

Of them is the hadith, allegedly, of 'Ali, and just listen to the hadith and you know something is wrong, where he says that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The month of Rajab is a magnificent month in the eyes of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Whoever fasts one day of the month of Rajab, Allah will write for him the fast of a thousand years." Mashallah, tabarakAllah. "And whoever fasts seven days, the doors of Jahannam are permanently shut for him. And whoever fasts fifteen days, all of his lifetime of evil shall be converted to good deeds, and an angel will cry out from the heavens: Allah has forgiven you." So it doesn't matter what you do now. You don't even need to be a scholar of hadith to say something is wrong with this hadith.

Now, where is it narrated? It is in a book that, I guarantee you, even the majority of 'ulama have never seen or heard of. It's one of the very obscure books: Ibn Shahin in his Fada'il. Ibn Shahin is a person who died 385 Hijrah. Al-Daraqutni says of him that he was a good man, but he made too many mistakes; he's not a person that we can rely on. Meaning he was a worshipper of Allah, but his memory was out there. So in these types of books you find these bizarre hadith about fasting Rajab.

And of course, of the things that are done in Rajab, culturally speaking, is that on the first Thursday night or Friday you have a special salah that is done in many cultures. A special salah: some people call it Salat al-Ragha'ib; others call it... what is it called? Can somebody help me, in Pakistan, what is it called? There's a term for it; I forgot. But you pray extra, and there's a special procedure, and you read this, and you read that 1,000 times, and there's an elaborate mechanism that is done. And al-Nawawi says this salah is a reprehensible bid'ah. In fact he says: "Bid'atun qabihatun munkaratun ashadd al-inkar." It is a reprehensible, weird, disgusting thing. It should never be done, and anybody who does it should be warned against, because there is a procedure to pray that is different than our prayers. It's weird: you do this, you do that, you recite this, you sit down. And Imam al-Nawawi says there is no basis for this thing. And this is the mainstream position: there is nothing special, no special salah, in Rajab.

How about if somebody wants to pray tahajjud in Rajab? Why should we prevent somebody from praying tahajjud? And again, that's what I'm saying (we talked about this before): if somebody wants to do a generic good deed, and he does it in a time frame that he thinks is maybe more rewarding, this is where the controversy occurs: is this bid'ah or not? And we should be lax. If somebody wants to pray tahajjud, normal tahajjud... What Imam al-Nawawi said is bid'ah is the bizarre prayer, which is a special technique: you sit down and you stand up and you do extra ruku' and sujud, like you pervert the prayer. He said this is weird, bid'ah, don't do it. But if somebody wants to pray genuine, legitimate tahajjud, should we say no? Okay, let him, alhamdulillah. It's better than me and you sleeping at night. At least he's doing some tahajjud. So no problem with that.

Now, another thing that people have a misconception about is that on one particular day (I think it's the 15th or something, they say) Isra' and Mi'raj took place, right? The 27th. See, I don't know the bid'ahs that well, I'm sorry; my knowledge of bid'ahs is a little bit weak. So they say that on the 27th of Rajab, Isra' and Mi'raj took place, and so they have extra deeds that they do over there. But from the books of seerah there is absolutely no indication that Isra' and Mi'raj took place in Rajab. In fact, if anything, al-Zuhri seems to indicate that it took place in Rabi' al-Awwal, and Zuhri is the authority of seerah; he died 127 Hijrah. And if anything, the most authentic thing that we have is that Isra' and Mi'raj took place in Rabi' al-Awwal. And even if it took place in Rajab, for us to do anything bizarre that is against the Sunnah (I'm not talking about a generic fast or tahajjud; this we can do any time), anything bizarre should not be done.

So this is the first part: **there doesn't seem to be any special actions that are required to do, or any special beliefs, of Rajab.** But if somebody wants to do any generic good deed, of generic sadaqah, of tahajjud, of fasting, they can do it in Rajab, and they can do it in any month. We should not cause an issue with that.
